{{Short description|Property of an iterated binary operation}}
{{Other uses|Telescope (disambiguation)}}

[[File:Telescop.svg|right|thumb|upright|The collapsing of a [[telescope]], in which successive segments slide into one another and disappear within the structure so that only the outermost parts remain visible, analogously illustrates telescoping in mathematics, where consecutive terms in algebraic expressions cancel each other out after expansion, leaving only the boundary terms.]]
In [[mathematics]], '''telescoping''' refers to a property of certain [[algebraic expressions]] or [[Iterated binary operation|iterated binary operations]] in which successive terms cancel each other after expansion. As a result, the overall expression simplifies significantly, since most intermediate terms eliminate one another, leaving only a small number of boundary terms from the original structure.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Telescoping Series - Product |website=Brilliant Math & Science Wiki |url=https://brilliant.org/wiki/telescoping-series-product/ |access-date=}}</ref>

Most commonly, expressions of the form

: <math>f(n)=g(n+1)-g(n)</math>

or

: <math>f(n)=\frac{g(n+1)}{g(n)},\quad g(n)\neq 0</math>

are considered, where <math>g</math> is a function defined on the set of [[natural numbers]].

== Definition ==

Let <math>A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}</math> and let <math>f,g:A\to \mathbb{R}</math>.

We say that a function <math>f</math> has the '''telescoping property''' with respect to <math>g</math> if one of the following holds:

=== Additive case ===

: <math>f(n)=g(n+1)-g(n)</math>.

Then the sum

: <math>\sum_{k=m}^{n} f(k)</math>

is telescoping.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |author=Eric W. Weisstein |title=Telescoping Sum |website=MathWorld |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/TelescopingSum.html |access-date=}}</ref>

=== Multiplicative case ===

If <math>g(n)\neq 0</math>, then

: <math>f(n)=\frac{g(n+1)}{g(n)}</math>.

Then the product

: <math>\prod_{k=m}^{n} f(k)</math>

reduces telescopically.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |author=Po-Shen Loh |title=Telescoping Sums and Products |date=2003-06-18 |url=https://www.math.cmu.edu/~lohp/docs/math/3-telescope-solns |access-date=}}</ref>

== Relation to finite difference operator ==

Let <math>\Delta</math> be the [[Finite-rank operator|finite difference operator]]:

: <math>\Delta g(n)=g(n+1)-g(n)</math>.

Then in the additive case:

: <math>f(n)=\Delta g(n)</math>.

This is analogous to the Newton–Leibniz formula:

: <math>\sum_{k=m}^{n}\Delta g(k)=g(n+1)-g(m)</math>.

Similarly for products:

: <math>\prod_{k=m}^{n}\frac{g(k+1)}{g(k)}=\frac{g(n+1)}{g(m)},\quad g(k)\neq 0</math>.

== Examples ==

=== [[Telescoping series|Telescoping sum]] ===

: <math>f(n)=\frac{1}{n(n+1)}</math>

Decomposition:

: <math>f(n)=\frac{1}{n}-\frac{1}{n+1}</math>

so for <math>g(n)=-\frac{1}{n}</math> we have

: <math>f(n)=g(n+1)-g(n)</math>.

Thus:

: <math>\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+1)}=1-\frac{1}{n+1}</math>.<ref name=":1" />

=== Telescoping product ===

: <math>f(n)=\frac{n+1}{n}</math>

with <math>g(n)=n</math>, so

: <math>\prod_{k=1}^{n}\frac{k+1}{k}=n+1</math>.<ref name=":2" />

=== Example with [[Fibonacci numbers]] ===

Let <math>F_n</math> be the Fibonacci sequence:

: <math>f(n)=\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}</math>.

Then:

: <math>\prod_{k=1}^{n}\frac{F_{k+1}}{F_k}=\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_1}=F_{n+1}</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Eric W. Weisstein |title=Fibonacci Number |website=MathWorld |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FibonacciNumber.html |access-date=}}</ref>
